text: Election day in Abuja. Amaka votes. The result is written on a sheet and stuck on the wall. Then it is read out, added up, and read out again at four more levels. At any step, can anyone prove the number is still the same? No. In 2023 the first sheet reached the portal at eight fifty-five at night, and the courts spent months arguing over paper. So we built Tally.

This is the polling unit. The presiding officer photographs the sheet. Tally reads the figures, she confirms them, and signs with her own phone. Now an agent from a rival party scans her code, checks it against the wall, and signs the same number. Two rivals agree, so the result is sealed. No network needed.
Anyone can see who signed. Amaka looks up her unit and hears the result in Hausa.

Now the part that matters. This is the ward, where numbers get read out and added up. I am the corrupt officer. I change one number, and announce it. Caught. In milliseconds. Tally names the unit. Announced a hundred and fifty, but agents of three parties signed fifty. Mission control goes red, and everyone following that unit gets the proof.

And it starts before the polls open. The store signs what it sends, the officer signs what arrives. Here, a unit is short of ballot papers. Found now, not in a queue. An elderly voter taps once for priority help. If nobody answers in fifteen minutes, mission control is told.
Someone forwards: A P C cheated. Tally does not take a side. It shows what was signed.
Everything except the ballot box, signed, witnessed and checkable. You can not rig it. Try.
